name: Rosa Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Rosa, and thanks for doing this. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union, party or government, and everything you say is confidential. Can you tell me what a normal working day looks like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a blast-hole drill at the Cerro Blanco lithium mine, out on the salt flats about forty minutes from town. The rig sits on tracks and I drill rows of holes, fifteen metres deep, to a pattern the engineers send to my screen, so the blasting crew can charge them. I'm the slowest driller on the bench, I'll tell you that straight, but I'm getting there. What I love is the morning, when the flats are pink and there's nobody but me and the rig. What wears me out is the wind, and the fact that I'm fifty-eight learning something the others learned at twenty.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up drilling at fifty-six?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was a care worker for twenty years and then I drove the school bus, and both paid nothing. When the lithium boom came the company ran a programme for older workers and women, so I applied. My partner Luis has bad lungs from welding and gets a small disability pension, and we spent our savings helping our daughter through her divorce last year. So we're starting from almost zero. I use the AI on my phone every day, by the way, to study the drill manuals and to check my maths on the patterns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, the tech bros oversold it, which is not a surprise. I'd probably post a joke about it in the union group chat. Then I'd say the real fight was always about pay and safety anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally it's fine, I'd keep using it for the little things it's good at. I'd still ask my phone to explain the drill manual at midnight, it just wouldn't be taking my job in the morning. I'd have time to become a good driller instead of a slow one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and push to get my next level ticket on the drill within a year, because that's a pay rise. I'd keep using AI to study. And I'd go back to helping the union with the newsletter, which I write with the AI's help now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit disappointed if I'm honest. I like new things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Disappointed? Why would you be disappointed if your job was safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because some of the new things are good. The autonomous drills they're testing at the other mine down the road are safer, no one breathing silica dust. I want the safety part, I just want us to keep our wages too. It's not the machine I'm against.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the next pay level mean for you and Luis in real money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a hundred and forty more a week. That's Luis's inhaler and the electricity, sorted. It would also mean we could start saving again, maybe a month's worth in a year if nothing breaks.

S0.say: She'd say the tech industry oversold AI, joke about it in the union chat, and argue that the real fight was always pay and safety.
S0.think: Privately she thinks the plateau is fine for her: AI stays a study helper and she gets time to become a good driller instead of a slow one.
S0.do: Keeps working and aims for the next drill ticket within a year, worth about a hundred and forty more a week. Keeps studying with AI and goes back to writing the union newsletter with its help.
S0.feel: Calm, and a little disappointed, because she enjoys new things.
S0.quote: I'd still ask my phone to explain the drill manual at midnight, it just wouldn't be taking my job in the morning.
S0.fieldNote: Rosa is the rare miner who feels a little let down by a plateau, because she sees safety benefits in automation and uses AI every day. She separates the machine from the deal: she wants the new tools but on terms that protect wages. Her money picture is very concrete, down to the inhaler and the electricity bill.

steps.text: Get the next level ticket on the blast-hole drill within a year
Keep studying the drill manuals and pattern maths with the phone AI
Go back to writing the union newsletter with the AI's help

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, let's get ahead of it, let's bargain for training now while the company still needs us. I'd write about it in the newsletter. I'd say the gains should be shared, not just go to the shareholders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, drilling to a pattern is exactly what a robot does well. The drill already knows where to go; I'm mostly there to watch it. I'm basically the babysitter for a machine that's already smarter than me about where to put the hole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight to the training office and ask about the remote operations centre in town, where they run the autonomous rigs. I'd do any course they offer, nights if needed, and use AI to study for it. And I'd get the union to make retraining a right in the next agreement, not a favour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but also a little excited. That's my personality, Luis says it'll get me in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're the slowest driller on the bench. Why do you think they'd pick you for the remote centre?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair question. I'm slow on the rig because my hands are slow, but on screens I'm quick, I've been using them every day for years. The young guys are better at feel, I'm better at reading what the system is telling me. I'd make that case, and if they still don't pick me, I'd go to the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut back on, if anything, during these years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably nothing big at first, we're already lean. Maybe I'd stop driving to see my daughter every weekend and do every second weekend. Petrol out there is not cheap.

S1.say: She'd urge colleagues to bargain for training while the company still needs them, write it up in the newsletter, and argue the gains should be shared with workers.
S1.think: She thinks her job, drilling to a computer pattern, is exactly what robots do well, and that she is already mostly a babysitter for the machine.
S1.do: Asks the training office about the remote operations centre and signs up for any course, studying at night with AI. Pushes the union to make retraining a right in the next agreement.
S1.feel: Uneasy, but also a little excited.
S1.quote: I'm basically the babysitter for a machine that's already smarter than me about where to put the hole.
S1.fieldNote: Rosa sees her own job clearly, admitting the rig already knows more than she does. Unusually for someone so new and slow on the controls, she has a credible case for a screen job and makes it confidently. Her instinct is to move first personally and to secure the same chance for everyone through the union.

steps.text: Ask the training office about the remote operations centre in town
Use AI as a tutor for any night course the mine offers
Get the union to make retraining a right in the next agreement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh. So the screen jobs go first. That's the ones I was aiming for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the newsletter I'd write that the remote operations centre is not a safe harbour any more, because that's thinking work and it goes in 2028. I'd say the hands-on jobs, maintenance, fitting, fixing the rigs, are the ones with three more years. And I'd say the company should train us for those now, on full pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd think my whole plan just turned upside down. I was going to sit at screens because my hands are slow, and now the screens are the first thing gone. Worse, the autonomous drills are already on trial down the road, so mine might not even wait for 2031. I'd be 60 with no savings and Luis on a disability pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd switch straight away from the remote centre to the maintenance crew, and ask to shadow the fitters on my days off. I'd use the AI every night to learn hydraulics and the drill's electrics, because that's hands-on work that lasts a bit longer. We'd sell the car and I'd get the mine bus, which saves about sixty a week. And I'd organise in the union for retraining on full pay, not a leaflet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, if I'm honest, and a bit angry. I'm good at learning, but I'm learning toward a door that's closing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think the fitters would take you on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Benny on the maintenance crew already lets me hand him spanners on night shift. He says I ask too many questions, which from Benny is a compliment. But they'd need fitters for three years and then not at all, so it's a short bridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen at home if the drill job went in 2029 or 2030?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Luis's pension pays for his medicine and not much else. We'd have to ask our daughter for a room, and she's only just back on her feet after the divorce. I'm quick to learn, but I can't learn my way out of having nothing in the bank.

S2.say: The remote operations centre is not a safe harbour any more, because that's thinking work and it goes in 2028. The hands-on jobs have three more years, and the company should train us for them now, on full pay.
S2.think: My whole plan turns upside down: I was going to sit at screens because my hands are slow, and the screens go first. The autonomous drills are already on trial down the road, so my rig might not even wait for 2031, and we have no savings.
S2.do: Switches her aim from the remote centre to the maintenance crew, shadowing the fitters on days off and using AI each night to learn hydraulics and drill electrics. Sells the car to save about sixty a week, and organises in the union for retraining on full pay.
S2.feel: Frightened and a bit angry, because she's learning toward a door that's closing.
S2.quote: I'm quick to learn, but I can't learn my way out of having nothing in the bank.
S2.fieldNote: Rosa's plan to move into the remote control room collapses under this card, because screen work goes first. She pivots at once to hands-on maintenance, which buys about three years, but knows autonomous drills on trial nearby may not wait. Being adaptable helps her move fast; it doesn't fix having no savings and a partner on a disability pension.

steps.text: Shadow the maintenance fitters on days off and study hydraulics with AI nightly
Sell the car and take the mine bus, saving about sixty a week
Organise in the union for retraining on full pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031 and 2034. Now that's a timeline I can do something with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the newsletter I'd say we've got five years before the screen jobs change and eight before the hands-on ones do, so there's no excuse for the company not training us. I'd push for a proper training fund. I'd want the older workers first in line, not last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be all right in this one. I'd be 63 when the computers come and 66 when the robots do, so I could do a diploma, work as a fitter for a few good years and retire before the robots reach the workshop. The only thing I'd worry about is the drills on trial nearby moving faster than the card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd enrol in a two-year night diploma in mechanical maintenance at the technical college, about 900 a year, and use AI as my tutor. I'd get the next drill ticket first so the extra 140 a week pays for it. And I'd save around thirty a week once the ticket comes through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly excited. I like a project, and this one has an end date I can live with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: 900 a year with no savings. How would you pay for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The next drill ticket pays for it, more or less. If the union wins a training fund, even better. I'd rather owe the college than owe nobody and know nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else would you want to bring along?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The women from the programme, there are six of us who started late. Give me five years and a laptop and I'll be the oldest fitter on the salt flats. I'd want the other five beside me.

S3.say: We've got five years before the screen jobs change and eight before the hands-on ones do, so there's no excuse for the company not training us. Older workers should be first in line, not last.
S3.think: I'd be all right in this one: a diploma, a few good years as a fitter, and retirement before the robots reach the workshop at 66. My worry is the drills on trial nearby moving faster than the card.
S3.do: Enrols in a two-year night diploma in mechanical maintenance at about 900 a year, with AI as a tutor. Gets the next drill ticket first so the extra 140 a week pays for it, and saves around thirty a week after that.
S3.feel: Uneasy but mostly excited, because the project has an end date she can live with.
S3.quote: Give me five years and a laptop and I'll be the oldest fitter on the salt flats.
S3.fieldNote: With five and eight years, Rosa's timeline lines up neatly with her retirement, and her mood lifts. She aims for hands-on maintenance rather than screen work, having understood which goes first. She wants to bring the other late-starting women with her.

steps.text: Enrol in a two-year night diploma in mechanical maintenance, about 900 a year
Use the phone AI as her tutor for the diploma
Save around thirty a week once the next drill ticket comes through

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2039? I'd be seventy-one. I'd be retired and nagging Luis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the picture for the young drillers, and the union should start the training fund now for them. Ten years is plenty if someone starts the clock. I'd write that in the newsletter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. I'd retire before either date, and my worry would move to my grandkids. I'm not racing the robots in this one, I'm just making sure they don't drive off with my pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get my next drill ticket, then start saving properly for the first time in years. I'd run an evening AI class for older workers at the union hall, because I'm already the one everyone asks. And I'd keep drilling till my pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a little sorry I won't see the cool part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean, making sure they don't drive off with your pension?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pension fund owns shares in mining companies. If robots make the company rich and the workers poor, I want the pension fund to get its slice. With ten years I'm not racing the robots anymore, I'm just making sure they don't drive off with my pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why teach a class if you're retiring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I like it, and because when I started at fifty-six nobody taught me anything slowly. An older worker who learns the AI at the union hall gets an extra few years at the mine. That's worth an evening a week.

S4.say: This is the picture for the young drillers, and the union should start the training fund now for them. Ten years is plenty if someone starts the clock.
S4.think: I'd be fine, retiring before either date, and my worry would move to my grandkids. I'm not racing the robots in this one.
S4.do: Gets her next drill ticket and starts saving properly for the first time in years. Runs an evening AI class for older workers at the union hall and keeps drilling until her pension.
S4.feel: Calm, and a little sorry she won't see the interesting part.
S4.quote: With ten years I'm not racing the robots anymore, I'm just making sure they don't drive off with my pension.
S4.fieldNote: With robots not due until 2039, Rosa expects to retire long before and turns outward, wanting to teach older colleagues. She still thinks about who gets the money from automation, down to her pension fund. Her mood here is the calmest of the AGI pictures.

steps.text: Get the next drill ticket and keep drilling until her pension
Save properly for the first time in years
Run an evening AI class for older workers at the union hall

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because the screen jobs I was aiming for go first and the drills soon after, and being clever doesn't help if there's no time. What would help is a training fund that pays you while you learn, not after, and a basic income floor so people like Luis and me don't fall through. Paid for by whoever owns the robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about safety. Everyone talks about jobs, but there are people breathing silica dust on the drills right now. If a robot can take the dust instead of my lungs, I want it, I just want my wage to come with me.

headlineQuote: If a robot can take the dust instead of my lungs, I want it, I just want my wage to come with me.
portrait: Rosa Nakamura is 58 and drills blast holes at the Cerro Blanco lithium mine, a job she took at fifty-six after twenty years in care work and a stint driving the school bus. She and her partner Luis, who has a small disability pension, spent their savings helping their daughter last year. She uses AI every day and sees safety gains in automation, so she's calm in a plateau and uneasy but eager in steady disruption. AGI by 2028 alarms her because the remote control room jobs she was aiming for are screen work that goes first, so she'd switch to hands-on maintenance, though autonomous drills on trial nearby may not wait. With five or ten years she plans a night diploma, expects to retire before the robots, and wants the union to win paid training for everyone.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because the screen jobs she'd aim for go first and the drills soon after, and being a quick learner wouldn't matter without time.
whatWouldHelp: A training fund that pays people while they learn, and a basic income floor, paid for by whoever owns the robots.
